lessons.title: decidir — to cut the question off
lessons.gloss: to decide — to cut a question off, and the verb every notice uses when it stops offering options

segments.text: Say ofrecer. The shop has offered you Thursday or Saturday. Say what you now have to do.
decidir — to decide. decidirse — to make up your mind.
Usted decide — you decide. It is what a notice says when it has finished offering and the choice is yours.
de- off, plus -cidir from Latin caedere, to cut. To cut the question off.
The same caedere is under a family that all involve cutting something away:

utterances: word: decidir. what is cut: the question.
word: preciso. what is cut: cut exactly to size.
word: conciso. what is cut: cut short.

segments.text: decidir and decidirse are not the same. Decido el menú is choosing a thing; me decido is the inner moment when you stop hesitating. Spanish marks that difference with the reflexive, where English leans on decide versus make up my mind.

segments.instruction: decidir
they offered me Thursday and I have to decide
segments.source: [YOU SAY: they offered me Thursday and I have to decide]

segments.instruction: the difference between decido and me decido
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the difference between *decido* and *me decido*]

segments.text: To decide? (decidir.) To make up your mind? (decidirse.) What does the Latin piece mean? (To cut.)

lessons.title: coincidir — to fall on the same day
lessons.gloss: to clash, to coincide — the reason people give for not coming, and a word your English eye can already read

segments.text: Say el grupo. Say decidir. The Tuesday group meets at the hour you already have something else. Name that problem.
coincidir — to coincide, and in everyday use to clash.
Me coincide con el trabajo — it clashes with work. That is the ordinary reason somebody gives for not taking a place.
co- together, plus the same -incidir family as decidir — things falling together.
Your English eye can read it without help, and that is the point worth taking:

But the everyday meaning has drifted. English coincide is neutral or lucky; Spanish coincidir, said about a timetable, is almost always a complaint. The form is transparent and the use is not, which is exactly where a confident reader gets caught.

segments.instruction: coincidir
it clashes with my work
segments.source: [YOU SAY: it clashes with my work]

segments.instruction: the Tuesday group clashes with my class
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the Tuesday group clashes with my class]

segments.text: To clash? (coincidir.) What does the co- add? (Together.) Is it usually good news? (No — about a timetable it is a complaint.)

lessons.title: equivocarse — when two things sound the same
lessons.gloss: to get it wrong — two Latin pieces meaning "equal voice", and the verb a shop uses to admit a mistake

segments.text: Say el pedido. The restaurant has sent two salads instead of a salad and a soup. Say what they did.
equivocarse — to be mistaken, to get it wrong.
Nos hemos equivocado — we have made a mistake. It is how a shop apologises without naming who is at fault.
aequus equal, plus vox voice. Equal voice — two things that sound the same and get taken for each other.
That is a precise picture of what a mistake is, and the same two pieces give you a word you may already recognise:

utterances: word: equivocarse. the equal voice in it: to confuse two things.
word: equívoco. the equal voice in it: ambiguous.

segments.text: It is almost always reflexive. You say me equivoco, not equivoco, because the error happens to you rather than being done to something else. Spanish uses that reflexive for a whole family of things that befall a person — caerse, olvidarse, perderse — and it is worth noticing as a group rather than memorising one at a time.

segments.instruction: equivocarse
we have made a mistake with the order
segments.source: [YOU SAY: we have made a mistake with the order]

segments.instruction: I was wrong
what the two Latin pieces mean
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what the two Latin pieces mean]

segments.text: To get it wrong? (equivocarse.) The two pieces? (Equal voice.) Which form do you use? (The reflexive — me equivoco.)

lessons.title: tardar — how long a thing takes
lessons.gloss: to take time — the verb the delay chapter promised and did not give you

segments.text: Say el retraso. That lesson mentioned a second word for lateness and did not teach it. Say it if you remember; here it is either way.
tardar — to take time, to be long about something.
Tardo una hora — it takes me an hour. ¿Cuánto tarda? — how long does it take?

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the delay and the duration

segments.text: el retraso and tardar are not interchangeable, and the difference is worth having exactly:

utterances: you mean: it is later than promised. you say: lleva retraso.
you mean: it takes this long. you say: tarda una hora.

segments.text: A journey that tarda two hours is not late — two hours is what the journey costs. A train with retraso has broken a promise. English blurs both into late and takes, and a reader who maps one to one will misread a station announcement.
Both come from tardus, slow, so the shared root is real and the split is recent.

segments.instruction: tardar
how long does it take?
segments.source: [YOU SAY: how long does it take?]

segments.instruction: it takes an hour and it is not late
segments.source: [YOU SAY: it takes an hour and it is not late]

segments.text: To take time? (tardar.) Later than promised? (con retraso.) Which one is a broken promise? (retraso.)

lessons.title: cenar — the meal as a verb
lessons.gloss: to have dinner — one verb where English needs three words, and the meal a plan usually ends at

segments.text: Say comer. You can say you eat. Say that you eat in the evening, and notice how many words English needs.
cenar — to have dinner, to dine. la cena is the meal itself.
Cenamos a las nueve — we have dinner at nine.
Spanish makes a verb out of each meal, where English has to say have plus a noun:

utterances: Spanish verb: desayunar. English needs: to have breakfast.
Spanish verb: comer. English needs: to have lunch.
Spanish verb: cenar. English needs: to have dinner.

segments.text: comer is the trap in that list. You already hold it as to eat, and in Spain it also means specifically to have lunch — ¿has comido? at four in the afternoon is asking whether you have had lunch, not whether you have eaten anything at all today.
So the three verbs are a set, and comer belongs to it as well as to the general sense.

segments.instruction: cenar
we have dinner at nine
segments.source: [YOU SAY: we have dinner at nine]

segments.instruction: the three meal verbs in order
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the three meal verbs in order]

segments.instruction: dinner takes an hour

segments.text: To have dinner? (cenar.) The meal itself? (la cena.) What else can comer mean in Spain? (To have lunch.)

lessons.title: (decidir, coincidir, equivocarse, tardar, cenar) — from cold
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of the five, and of the reflexive that marks what happens to you

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say all five: to decide, to clash, to get it wrong, to take time, to have dinner.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the reflexive marks what happens to you

utterances: plain: decido. reflexive: me decido. the difference: choosing a thing vs making up your mind.
plain: equivoco. reflexive: me equivoco. the difference: the error befalls you.

segments.text: equivocarse is almost never plain, because a mistake is something that happens to a person. The same shape covers caerse, olvidarse and perderse — a family worth noticing together rather than one at a time.
coincidir takes no reflexive and still points at you: me coincide uses the indirect pronoun, not the reflexive, because the clash is reported to you rather than done by you.

Seven chapters ago you could name things. You can now arrange an evening and say what went wrong with it. You can be offered two dates, decide, say the other one clashes, admit a mistake, say how long something takes and name the meal at the end of it.
tardar closes a debt: the chapter on delays mentioned it in passing and did not teach it, and a word shown but never given is one a reader half-knows.

segments.text: To clash? (coincidir.) To get it wrong? (equivocarse.) To take time? (tardar.) To decide? (decidir.) To have dinner? (cenar.)

lessons.title: (cambiar un plan) — read it, then do it yourself
lessons.gloss: the payoff — read a message that changes a plan, then change one yourself

segments.text: Say coincidir and decidir. The message you are about to read turns on both.
Read it once straight through, then answer.
Hola: al final no puedo el jueves, me coincide con el curso. Perdona, me equivoqué de semana al apuntarlo. ¿Cenamos el viernes? Yo tardo media hora en llegar, así que sobre las nueve.

segments.text: Every sentence there is an ordinary message between two friends, and none of it was sayable seven chapters ago — not because the grammar was missing, but because the verbs were.
It clashes? (me coincide.) I got it wrong? (me equivoqué.) Shall we have dinner? (¿cenamos?)
